deck: 20 Head First Java::03 Know Your Variables

cards.front: What must every variable declaration contain?
cards.extra: Java is statically typed, so int size; tells the compiler the cup's shape before any value exists. Without the type the compiler cannot check assignments.

cards.front: int x = 24; byte b = x; — why does this not compile?
cards.back: The compiler checks types, not the current value; a cast is required
cards.extra: It knows an int may hold values that do not fit a byte, and refuses to guess. byte b = (byte) x; compiles — and silently truncates for larger values.

cards.front: What does a primitive variable hold, and what does a reference variable hold?
cards.back: Primitive: the value itself. Reference: bits that get you to an object
cards.extra: 5, -26.7, 'a' are values. A reference is more like a remote control: you cannot see inside it, and you cannot do arithmetic on it.

cards.front: Is there such a thing as an object variable in Java?
cards.extra: The variable holds a way to access an object, never the object's bytes. That is why two variables can name the same object and why assignment never copies it.

cards.front: Book c = new Book(); Book d = c; — how many objects exist?
cards.back: One — d copies the reference, not the object
cards.extra: Both variables hold identical bits pointing at the same heap object. Changing a field through d is visible through c.

cards.front: Book b = new Book(); Book c = new Book(); b = c; — count references and objects afterwards
cards.extra: The first object loses its only name when b is overwritten, so it becomes collectable. The reference count is unchanged; the reachable object count dropped.

cards.front: An array variable such as int[] nums holds what?
cards.back: A reference to an array object on the heap
cards.extra: nums = new int[7]; creates the array object and points the variable at it. The variable itself is still just a remote control.

cards.front: new Dog[7] — how many Dog objects have been created?
cards.extra: Creating the array allocates the tray, not the dogs. Each slot must be filled with new Dog() before use, otherwise you get a NullPointerException.

cards.front: How do you call a method on a Dog stored in an array?
cards.extra: The element expression evaluates to a reference, and the dot works on that. The classic bug is myDogs.bark(), which treats the array itself as the object.

cards.front: Do the elements of a Dog[] hold Dog objects or references?
cards.back: References — the objects live elsewhere on the heap
cards.extra: This is why two slots can point at the same dog and why assigning myDogs[2] = dog1; creates no new object.
